concepts.name: State the goal before any metric
Tie each metric to a user action
Pick what matters most and say why
Prefer a count for the North Star
Set guardrails that must not fall
Use override rate as the trust signal
Separate secondary metrics from business metrics
Say exactly how each metric is collected
Rule out boring causes before a product theory
Split the drop by region and platform
Check whether your own product absorbed the traffic

cards.title: Start with the goal
cards.body: GAME is a four-step way to answer "How would you measure success?": Goals, Actions, Metrics, Evaluations. Start with G: say what the product is trying to accomplish before naming a single metric. Without a goal, you can't judge which metrics matter.
cards.example: A recipe app's Save button. Goal: help people actually cook the recipes they find, not just browse them.

cards.title: List what users can do
cards.body: A is Actions: the things users can actually do with the product. Listing actions keeps your metrics tied to real behavior instead of vague ideas like "engagement".
cards.example: Save a recipe. Open a saved recipe. Cook from it. Share it.
cards.source: wiki: GAME (A); C-NABGT note that "we'd track engagement" is unacceptable

cards.title: Count each action
cards.body: M is Metrics: for each action, name something you can count. A good metric is specific enough that a data scientist could write the query straight away.
cards.example: Save: recipes saved per weekly user. Cook: share of saved recipes opened in cooking mode within 7 days.
cards.source: wiki: GAME (M); C-NABGT note that a data scientist must be able to write the SQL

cards.title: Pick what matters and say why
cards.body: E is Evaluations: decide which metrics matter most for the goal, and explain why. Then land on a clear answer. Interviewers mark down "it depends".
cards.example: Most important: share of saved recipes cooked within 7 days. It shows the goal is happening. Saves alone don't.
cards.source: wiki: GAME (E); evaluation criterion 5, recommendation clarity

quiz.prompt: An interviewer asks how you'd measure the success of Instagram Reels. What should you say first?
options: A list of engagement metrics like DAU and time spent
What Reels is trying to accomplish
Which metric is the North Star
How Reels makes money
quiz.explanation: Goals come first. Until you know what Reels is for, you can't tell which metrics matter.

quiz.statement: Opening with standard metrics like DAU and time spent is fine, as long as they're the metrics the company already tracks.
quiz.explanation: Standard metrics without a goal are guesses. State the goal first, then choose metrics that show it's being met.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a metric you could actually count?
options: Users love saving recipes
Engagement with the Save button
Recipes saved per weekly active user
Brand affinity
quiz.explanation: It names a specific action (saving) and a specific count. A data scientist could write the query straight away.

quiz.prompt: Match each user action to a metric that counts it.

pairs.right: Share of saved recipes opened in cooking mode

quiz.explanation: Each metric counts one specific thing a user does. That's what makes it measurable.

quiz.statement: "We'd track engagement" is a specific enough metric for an interview answer.
quiz.explanation: Engagement isn't countable as stated. Name the action and the count, like recipes saved per weekly user.

quiz.prompt: What does the E in GAME ask you to do?
options: Estimate the size of the market
Decide which metrics matter most, and why
Explain how the feature was built
Experiment with an A/B test
quiz.explanation: E is Evaluations: rank your metrics against the goal and justify the top one.

quiz.prompt: You've listed six metrics. What's the strongest next move?
options: Say you'd track all six equally
Add a few more to be thorough
Pick the one that best shows the goal is met, and explain why
Pick the one that's easiest to measure
quiz.explanation: Listing is only half the job. Strong answers choose and justify.

quiz.statement: Ending with "it depends on the company's priorities" is a safe, strong close.
quiz.explanation: Interviewers want you to land somewhere specific. Make a call and give the reason.

fixWeakAnswer.question: How would you measure the success of a new "Save for later" button in a news app?
fixWeakAnswer.weakAnswer: I'd look at DAU, time spent in the app, and the number of saves. If all three go up after launch, the feature is a success.

weakParts.text: I'd look at DAU, time spent in the app
weakParts.label: Generic metrics with no goal

weakParts.text: If all three go up after launch, the feature is a success.
weakParts.label: No pick, no reason

fixWeakAnswer.instructions: Rewrite this answer using GAME. State the goal, tie your metrics to what users do, and pick the one that matters most.

checklist.criterion: States what the Save for later button is trying to achieve, before naming metrics
Names at least two specific user actions, such as saving an article and coming back to read it
Gives a countable metric for each action, not generic DAU or time spent
Picks the most important metric and says why it shows the goal is met

voice.question: How would you measure the success of Spotify's Discover Weekly playlist?

evaluationRubric.excellent: States the goal first, ties each metric to a specific user action, then picks one metric and justifies it against the goal
evaluationRubric.good: Clear goal and action-based metrics, but no clear pick or a weak justification
evaluationRubric.fair: Reasonable metrics, but no stated goal or no link to user actions
evaluationRubric.poor: Generic metrics only (DAU, engagement, time spent) with no structure

keyPoints: Goal stated before metrics, e.g. help listeners discover new music they keep coming back to
Specific user actions: open the playlist, play tracks, save or like a track, follow an artist
A countable metric for each action
One metric picked as most important, with the reason it shows the goal is met

conceptChecks.criterion: States what Discover Weekly is trying to accomplish before naming metrics
Names specific user actions (opening the playlist, playing, saving tracks) with a countable metric for each
Picks the most important metric and explains why

cards.title: Anchor on one North Star
cards.body: SIGNAL extends GAME for AI products: Scope, Identify the goal, Generate metrics, Negative guardrails, Anchor on a North Star, Layer breakdowns. The North Star is the one number that shows users are getting real value.
cards.example: An AI writing assistant: weekly active users who complete a task with it.
cards.source: wiki: SIGNAL (all steps, A); North Star example

cards.title: Prefer a count
cards.body: Prefer a count for your North Star. A ratio can rise when its denominator shrinks: if users who aren't getting value leave, the rate climbs while the product shrinks. Ratios still work as supporting metrics.
cards.example: 300 of 1,000 users complete a task: 30%. Then 500 who never did leave: 300 of 500 is 60%. The count stayed at 300.
cards.source: wiki: SIGNAL, North Star must be an absolute count, never a ratio alone

cards.title: Set guardrails
cards.body: N is Negative guardrails: metrics that must not get worse while you push the North Star. They catch wins that quietly cost something else, like quality, speed or money.
cards.example: Pushing AI answers to more questions? Guard hallucination rate, response time and cost per query.
cards.source: wiki: SIGNAL (N); key AI metrics list

cards.title: Watch what users override
cards.body: User override rate is how often users correct or dismiss the AI's output. It's a more honest trust signal than accuracy, because it measures what users actually do, not how the model scored in testing.
cards.example: 95% accuracy in testing, but users edit or delete 60% of drafts. They don't trust it yet.
cards.source: wiki: SIGNAL, user override rate is a more honest trust signal than accuracy

quiz.prompt: Which is the strongest North Star for an AI writing assistant?
options: Average suggestions accepted per user
Weekly users who complete a task with the assistant
Model accuracy on a test set
Total suggestions shown
quiz.explanation: It's a count of people getting real value. An average can rise just because less engaged users left.

quiz.statement: A ratio North Star can improve even while the product is losing users.
quiz.explanation: If the users who leave are in the denominator but not the numerator, the ratio goes up as the product shrinks.

quiz.statement: Ratios have no place in a metrics answer.
quiz.explanation: Ratios are useful supporting metrics. Just prefer a count for the North Star, and read ratios alongside it.

quiz.prompt: What is a guardrail metric?
options: The metric you're trying to grow
A metric that must not get worse while you push the North Star
A metric only engineers track
A metric you report to investors
quiz.explanation: Guardrails are the things you refuse to sacrifice while chasing the main goal.

quiz.prompt: Match each push to the guardrail that protects against its risk.

pairs.left: Run the AI on every message instead of on request
Let the AI answer more questions on its own

quiz.explanation: Each push has a predictable cost. The guardrail is the metric that would show it.

quiz.statement: Once the North Star is going up, guardrails don't matter much.
quiz.explanation: That's exactly when they matter. A rising North Star can hide a quality, speed or cost problem.

quiz.prompt: What does user override rate measure?
options: How often the model is updated
How often users correct or dismiss the AI's output
How often the AI refuses a request
How often admins change settings
quiz.explanation: It counts real user behavior: edits, dismissals and rejections.

quiz.prompt: An AI drafting tool scores 95% accuracy in testing, but users edit or delete 60% of its drafts. Which is the more honest trust signal?
options: The 95% accuracy, because it's measured objectively
The 60% override rate, because it shows what users actually do
Neither, because trust can't be measured
Average draft length
quiz.explanation: Accuracy is measured in testing. Overrides show whether real users trust the output enough to use it.

fixWeakAnswer.question: How would you measure the success of an AI that drafts replies for agents in a customer support tool?
fixWeakAnswer.weakAnswer: Our North Star is average CSAT on tickets where agents use the AI draft. As long as that goes up, the feature is working, so we'd push agents to use drafts on as many tickets as possible.

weakParts.text: Our North Star is average CSAT on tickets where agents use the AI draft.
weakParts.label: Average as the North Star, with no count

weakParts.text: As long as that goes up, the feature is working
weakParts.label: No guardrails

weakParts.text: so we'd push agents to use drafts on as many tickets as possible.
weakParts.label: Pushes volume with no check on whether agents trust the drafts

fixWeakAnswer.instructions: Rewrite this answer using SIGNAL. Anchor on a count, set at least one guardrail, and show how you'd know agents trust the drafts.

checklist.criterion: Uses a count as the North Star (such as weekly agents who send an AI-drafted reply), or explains why an average alone could mislead
Names at least one guardrail that must not get worse, such as hallucination rate, escalations or cost per query
Says what the guardrail protects against when agents use drafts on more tickets
Includes override rate: how often agents heavily edit or discard the AI's draft

voice.question: How would you measure the success of an AI feature that summarizes long email threads?

evaluationRubric.excellent: Anchors on a count-based North Star tied to real value, names one or two guardrails that must not fall, and uses override or correction behavior as the trust signal
evaluationRubric.good: Count-based North Star and at least one guardrail, but no trust signal or thin reasoning
evaluationRubric.fair: Reasonable metrics, but a ratio or average North Star with no caveat, or no guardrails
evaluationRubric.poor: Model accuracy or generic engagement only, with no North Star

keyPoints: A North Star that counts people getting value, e.g. weekly users who act on a thread after reading only its summary
Why a count over a ratio: a rate can rise as users leave
Guardrails such as hallucination rate (the summary misstates the thread), time-to-first-token, or cost per query
A trust signal from user behavior: opening the full thread right after the summary, or flagging and editing summaries

conceptChecks.criterion: Anchors on a count-based North Star, or explains why a ratio alone could mislead
Names at least one guardrail that must not get worse, and what it protects
Uses a user-behavior trust signal, such as override rate or reopening the full thread

cards.title: The full answer, scope first
cards.body: C-NABGT is the full structure for an AI metrics answer: Clarify scope, North Star, Actionable secondary metrics, Business metrics, Guardrails, Tracking plan. You met N and G in lesson 2. C comes first: which product, which users, what time window.
cards.example: AI photo editor: mobile users, not pro desktop users. Weekly metrics at launch.
cards.source: wiki: C-NABGT (all steps, C); SIGNAL (S = product, users, time window)

cards.title: Secondary metrics the team can act on
cards.body: A is 2–3 actionable secondary metrics. They explain why the North Star moved and point the team to what to fix.
cards.example: Photo editor: edits completed per session, share of AI edits kept without undo, export rate.

cards.title: Business metrics, kept separate
cards.body: B is Business metrics: revenue, cost and unit economics. They show whether the product works for the company, not just for users. Keep them apart from secondary metrics: one tells the team what to fix, the other tells leadership whether it pays.
cards.example: Photo editor: upgrades to the paid plan, cost per AI edit.
cards.source: wiki: C-NABGT (B = revenue, cost, unit economics)

cards.title: Define every metric
cards.body: T is the Tracking plan: how each metric is actually collected. It's the step that separates strong answers from weak ones. Define each metric precisely enough that a data scientist could write the query.
cards.example: "AI edit kept" = an AI edit applied and not undone within 60 seconds, logged as an app event.
cards.source: wiki: C-NABGT (T separates strong from weak; data scientist must be able to write the SQL)

cards.title: Method and cadence
cards.body: Not every metric comes from logs. For each one, say how it's measured (logged events, automated evals or human raters) and how often.
cards.example: Hallucination rate: weekly human-rated sample of 500 outputs. Cost per edit: daily, from billing data.
cards.source: wiki: C-NABGT (T = human raters? automated evals? what cadence?)

quiz.prompt: You're asked how you'd measure an AI meeting-notes feature. What does Clarify scope cover?
options: How the model was trained
Which product, which users and what time window you're measuring
The company's revenue target
Which metrics to leave out
quiz.explanation: Scope sets the boundaries, so every metric that follows means one clear thing.

quiz.statement: "Weekly active users" means the same thing whether you're measuring the consumer app or the developer API.
quiz.explanation: Different products and users make the same metric mean different things. That's why scope comes first.

quiz.prompt: For an AI meeting-notes feature, match each C-NABGT step to an example.

pairs.right: Notes shared after the meeting, per meeting
Rate of action items assigned to the wrong person

quiz.explanation: Each step has a different job. Mixing them up is how answers get muddled.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a business metric?
options: Notes shared per meeting
Cost per summary generated
Hallucination rate
Share of summaries edited before sharing
quiz.explanation: Cost is unit economics. The others describe user behavior or quality.

quiz.statement: Revenue makes a good actionable secondary metric for the feature team.
quiz.explanation: Revenue is a business metric. Secondary metrics should point the team to something it can change directly.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a usable tracking-plan definition?
options: We'd track engagement
We'd instrument the UI
"Summary shared" = user taps Share on a summary within 24 hours of the meeting, logged as an app event
We'd check the dashboard regularly
quiz.explanation: It names the exact event, the time window and the data source. A data scientist could write the query.

quiz.statement: Every metric in an AI metrics answer can be tracked from app logs.
quiz.explanation: Quality metrics like hallucination rate usually need automated evals or human raters.

quiz.prompt: How would you track hallucination rate for AI meeting summaries?
options: Total summaries generated per week
A weekly human-rated sample of summaries checked against the meeting transcript
Average summary length
Number of users who open the feature
quiz.explanation: It names the method (human raters), the check (against the transcript) and the cadence (weekly).

fixWeakAnswer.question: How would you measure the success of an AI feature that writes product descriptions for online sellers?
fixWeakAnswer.weakAnswer: North Star: weekly sellers who publish an AI-written description. We'd also look at revenue and engagement, keep hallucinations low, and track everything in a dashboard.

weakParts.text: North Star: weekly sellers who publish an AI-written description.
weakParts.label: Jumps to the North Star with no scope

weakParts.text: We'd also look at revenue and engagement
weakParts.label: Business and secondary metrics blurred, and "engagement" isn't defined

weakParts.text: and track everything in a dashboard.
weakParts.label: No tracking plan: no definition, method or cadence

fixWeakAnswer.instructions: Rewrite this answer using C-NABGT. Clarify scope, separate secondary and business metrics, and say how at least one metric is collected.

checklist.criterion: Clarifies scope first: which sellers or marketplace, and what time window
Names 1–2 actionable secondary metrics the team can move, such as share of AI descriptions published without edits
Names a business metric separately, such as cost per description or sales on listings with AI descriptions
Defines how at least one metric is collected (logged event, automated eval or human rating) and how often

voice.question: How would you measure the success of an AI trip planner that builds travel itineraries?

evaluationRubric.excellent: Clarifies scope, anchors on a count-based North Star, separates actionable secondary metrics from business metrics, sets an AI guardrail, and gives a tracking plan with method and cadence for the key metrics
evaluationRubric.good: Covers most of C-NABGT, but the tracking plan is vague ("we'd instrument it") or secondary and business metrics are blurred
evaluationRubric.fair: Reasonable metrics but no scope and no tracking plan, or a ratio North Star with no count or caveat
evaluationRubric.poor: Generic engagement or satisfaction with no definitions

keyPoints: Scope: which travelers, which product surface, what time window
A count-based North Star, e.g. weekly users who book at least one item from an AI itinerary
Secondary metrics (e.g. share of itinerary items kept without edits) kept separate from business metrics (e.g. booking revenue, cost per itinerary)
An AI guardrail, e.g. rate of wrong itinerary items (closed venues, impossible timings)
A tracking plan: definition, method (events, evals, human raters) and cadence for the key metrics

conceptChecks.criterion: Clarifies which users, product and time window before naming metrics
Names secondary and business metrics separately, with at least one of each
Says how at least one key metric is collected and how often

cards.title: Boring causes first
cards.body: When a metric drops, don't jump to a product theory. First confirm the data: a logging bug or a seasonal dip can look like a real drop. Then work through TROPIC: Time, Region, Other launches, Platform, Industry, Cannibalization.
cards.example: Bookings fell 8% on Monday. Did the tracking change, or was it a holiday week?
cards.source: wiki: TROPIC (rule out boring causes first; anti-pattern: skipping data pipeline errors or seasonal effects)

cards.title: Time, other launches, industry
cards.body: T: was the drop sudden or gradual? Sudden often points to a release or a bug. O: did something else ship at the same time? I: are competitors seeing it too? If so, the cause probably isn't your product.
cards.example: Overnight drop on release day: check the release. Slow decline across the industry: look at the market.

cards.title: Region and platform
cards.body: R and P split the drop. Is it global, or one market? Every platform, or just iOS? A drop confined to one segment points straight at what changed there.
cards.example: Drop only on Android in Brazil: check the latest Android build and anything that changed in that market.

cards.title: Cannibalization
cards.body: C is Cannibalization: did one of your own products absorb the traffic? A drop in one place can be a shift, not a loss. Check whether a related product grew by about the same amount.
cards.example: Feed posts drop 10% the month Stories launches, while story posts rise. Users moved, they didn't leave.

cards.title: Add the AI layer
cards.body: For AI products, always add one more check: did the model update silently? Did response time spike? Did the hallucination or error rate rise and push users away? Lesson 5 goes deeper.
cards.example: AI assistant usage drops the day after a model swap: compare quality and speed before and after.
cards.source: wiki: TROPIC (AI-specific layer, always add this)

quiz.prompt: Daily orders dropped 15% yesterday. What's your first move?
options: Launch a win-back campaign
Check whether the data is right, such as a logging or pipeline change
Interview users who stopped ordering
Roll back the latest feature
quiz.explanation: Rule out boring causes first. A broken pipeline can look exactly like a real drop.

quiz.statement: If competitors saw the same drop in the same week, the cause is probably outside your product.
quiz.explanation: That's the I in TROPIC: an industry-wide drop points to the market, not your product.

quiz.prompt: Match each check to the question it asks.

pairs.right: Did something else ship at the same time?

quiz.explanation: Each check rules out one boring cause before you reach for a product theory.

quiz.prompt: Signups dropped 12%. Split by platform: iOS is down 40%, Android and web are flat. What's your next step?
options: Redesign the signup flow on every platform
Look at what changed on iOS, such as a new app release or an OS update
Assume it's seasonal
Check competitor signups
quiz.explanation: The segment tells you where to look. Something changed on iOS.

quiz.statement: Splitting the drop by region and platform is only worth doing once you've decided on the cause.
quiz.explanation: Segment first. Where the drop is tells you what to investigate.

quiz.prompt: Web visits fell 10% the month your new mobile app launched, and app sessions rose by about the same amount. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The website has a bug
Users moved from web to the app
Users are leaving the product
A competitor launched
quiz.explanation: That's cannibalization: the traffic shifted between your own products.

quiz.statement: A drop caused by cannibalization always means the business is losing users.
quiz.explanation: Users may have just moved to another of your products. Check the total across both.

quiz.prompt: Weekly users of an AI assistant fell 9% right after a model update. Which check belongs to the AI layer?
options: Check whether competitors saw the same drop
Compare hallucination rate and response time before and after the update
Split the drop by region
Send a re-engagement email
quiz.explanation: The AI layer asks whether the model itself got worse. The other checks are useful, but they belong to other TROPIC steps or aren't checks at all.

fixWeakAnswer.question: Weekly active users of a food-delivery app dropped 10% last week. How would you investigate?
fixWeakAnswer.weakAnswer: The new checkout redesign shipped two weeks ago, so that's probably the cause. I'd roll it back everywhere and survey users about what they dislike. Our new grocery app launched last week too, but that's a separate product.

weakParts.text: The new checkout redesign shipped two weeks ago, so that's probably the cause.
weakParts.label: Jumps to a product theory without ruling out boring causes
Acts before finding which region or platform dropped

weakParts.text: Our new grocery app launched last week too, but that's a separate product.
weakParts.label: Ignores possible cannibalization

fixWeakAnswer.instructions: Rewrite this answer using TROPIC. Rule out boring causes, split the drop, and check whether your own product absorbed the traffic.

checklist.criterion: Checks the data and boring causes first: tracking changes, seasonality, or whether competitors dropped too
Checks whether the drop's timing matches a release (the redesign shipped a week before the drop)
Splits the drop by region or platform before acting
Checks whether the new grocery app absorbed the traffic

voice.question: Daily active users of a music streaming app dropped 8% last week. How would you investigate?

evaluationRubric.excellent: Confirms the data first, rules out boring causes (timing, other launches, industry), splits the drop by region and platform, checks cannibalization, and only then forms a product theory
evaluationRubric.good: Systematic and splits the drop, but skips the data check or cannibalization
evaluationRubric.fair: Some checks, but jumps to a product theory early
evaluationRubric.poor: Proposes a fix right away with no investigation

keyPoints: Confirm the data: tracking or pipeline changes, seasonality
Timing: sudden or gradual, and whether it lines up with a release or another launch
Cannibalization: did another of the company's products, such as a podcast app, absorb the listening?

conceptChecks.criterion: Rules out boring causes (data, timing, other launches or industry) before any product theory
Splits the drop by region or platform
Checks whether another of the company's own products absorbed the usage
